title: Expectation shapes
hookLine: expectation changes experience, which isn't fake, it's how minds work

cards: Here's a strange experiment. A doctor hands a patient a bottle of pills and says, plainly: these are sugar pills. There's no medicine in them.
We're telling you that honestly. Take them twice a day anyway. That happened, in a study at Harvard in 2010, with people who had a painful gut condition.
Three weeks later, many of the people taking the pills they knew were fake reported that their symptoms had eased more than people who got nothing at all. Nobody was fooled. So what was going on?

teach.b: The word placebo is Latin: I will please. In medicine, it's a treatment with no active ingredient.
Researchers have long known that people often feel better after one, especially with pain, nausea and other symptoms the brain helps produce.
The honest-pill study, led by Ted Kaptchuk, suggested that the ritual of treatment and the expectation of care matter, even without deception.

That isn't imagining things, and it doesn't mean the symptoms were fake. Expectation works through the same brain and body that feel everything else. Pain is real, and so is the brain's part in shaping it.
And it has limits: expectation doesn't shrink tumors or mend bones. No magic.

teach.h: WHAT WE'RE TOLD SHIFTS WHAT WE FEEL.
teach.b: In everyday life, researchers have found that what people are told about something, like whether a food is indulgent or healthy, or whether their work counts as exercise, can shift how they experience it.
Some of those findings are small or contested, so hold them lightly; the older placebo research is the firmer ground. The old voices each said it their own way.
Marcus Aurelius, in George Long's translation: "The universe is transformation: life is opinion." For the Stoics, it isn't events that disturb people but their judgments about them.
The Dhammapada opens with the Buddha's teaching that lives are shaped by the mind. Different traditions, different reasons, each in its own house.
And the week behind you: sublimis, take it for a walk somewhere green, the stone in your shoe, a mirror, not a forecast, the self can step aside, move.
Some of how they help may come through what you expect, alongside what they do for the body. That wouldn't make them fake. It's how minds work.

how: Researchers study expectation through placebo and framing experiments; in daily life many people notice and name their expectations before an event, a practice echoed in Stoic reflection.

o: if you believe hard enough, anything can be cured
sugar pills only work when patients are fooled
what you expect can change what you actually feel

s: a placebo only works if you're fooled
in the 2010 study, people knew the pills were sugar and many still felt better.
expectation works through the same brain and body that feel everything else
that's why placebo effects aren't fake: they're how minds work.
expectation can cure anything if you believe hard enough

games.q: a doctor hands you pills and says honestly: these are sugar. take them anyway. what happened in the study?
o: many reported their symptoms eased more than those with no pills.
games.why: in Kaptchuk's 2010 study, open-label placebo helped many people with a gut condition feel better, without deception.

practice: Think of one thing coming up soon, a meeting, a meal, a visit, a chore, and name what you're already expecting from it: boring, awful, wonderful. Then hold it a bit more loosely and ask what's one other way it could go.
You're not forcing yourself to be positive, just noticing the expectation shaping things before anything has happened.

wordCard.voice: Expectation shapes. What you expect changes what you experience, not because it's fake, but because that's how minds and bodies work.

orig.note: Latin: I will please; the first word of a psalm verse sung in the old office for the dead.

carryVoice: Your line: expecting shapes. Within limits, and never by magic. A week done, and day three hundred twenty-two.
